chapters.text: Hi! I'm Priya. I cycle to the hospital every morning, and the ring road scares me half to death. One safe route would change my whole week.
The safe streets mean my neighbour's kids now ride to school alongside me. We call ourselves the 7:40 convoy.
I sold the car I hardly used and took my mum to the seaside by train with the money. Getting around Willowbrook is easy now.
Edith here, plot 14. I've grown runner beans on this allotment for forty years. Half the plots stand empty now, and the young ones don't know where to start.
The compost point is a marvel. Young Sam from plot 9 asked me how to make leaf mould, so now I teach on Saturdays. Tea provided.
There's a waiting list for plots again! We sent forty jars of chutney to the food market. I've never been so busy, or so happy.
Morning! Rafael, from the corner shop on Market Street. The supermarket on the bypass took most of my customers. I'd love to sell local food, if only I could find any.
Saturdays at the food market are wonderful chaos. I buy apples from Orchard Lane and eggs from Northfield, and people are coming back to the high street.
My daughter wants to take over the shop one day. Ten years ago I'd have told her to leave town. Now I tell her Willowbrook is going places.
Joe, from the old mill. The heating bills here would make you weep, and half our kit gets thrown out the moment it breaks.
Turns out I'm good at fixing toasters. Every other Thursday I run a bench at the repair café, and people bring me cake.
The energy co-op put panels on the mill roof. The lads joke that we finally make something cleaner than smoke. Proud of that, I am.
I'm Amara, I teach Year 4. My class drew maps of their walk to school. Most of them drew cars. Only one drew a tree.
With the safe streets in, we walk to school as a 'walking bus'. The children count birds on the way. Yesterday's record: eleven.
This year the children drew their maps again. They're full of trees, flowers and one very large hedgehog. I've pinned it by my desk.
Nadia, fourth floor. I work nights. In winter our flat is so cold the windows stream with water, and my son's cough never quite goes away.
They insulated our block! The draught under the door has gone and the damp patch in the bedroom is drying out. I slept right through the afternoon.
Our energy bill is half what it was. My son hasn't coughed all winter. The money we save goes in a jar marked 'holiday'.
Tom, Northfield Farms. Fourth generation. Money's tight, the soil is tired, and I'm not sure my kids will want this life.
Left the field edges wild this year, like you suggested. The skylarks are back over the barley and the bees are doing half my work.
I sell straight to the town market now. Better price, and I know who eats my food. My daughter's studying soil science. Reckon she'll be back.

residents.name: Leo
residents.role: Aged nine, lives by the weir

chapters.text: My name is Leo and I am nine. Mum says when I was little the river came into our garden. I want to see an otter but Grandad says they're all gone.
We planted a rain garden at the end of our road. When it rains it fills up like a bath, then soaks away slowly. Our garden stays dry now.
I SAW AN OTTER!!! It was by the weir eating a fish. Grandad cried a bit. He says he hasn't seen one since he was my age.
